articles.title: Wired Warns: Encryption Under Global Attack
articles.content: Save Story Save this story Save Story Save this story Welcome to Kernel Panic , a weekly newsletter by Lily Hay Newman and Matt Burgess from inside the new world of privacy and digital security. To receive this newsletter in your inbox each week, sign up here . Oh, Canada. The Great White North is the latest country to contemplate legislation that could essentially mandate backdoors and increase data retention in encrypted services. The proposed changes have prompted the Canadian anti-censorship company Psiphon VPN—which keeps millions of Iranians online during repressive internet shutdowns —to say it will leave the country if the bill passes. And Psiphon is not the only one. Encrypted messaging app Signal has said it would exit the Canadian market because the legislation would require unacceptable changes to its open source projects. Apple and Meta have criticized the bill, and DuckDuckGo and NordVPN say they would consider pulling their services, too. But as countries around the world contemplate similar legislation, even larger questions begin to emerge about which states or regions could differentiate themselves as being safe havens for privacy services if global hostility to encryption continues to rise. It’s been maddening and disturbing to see more and more democratic countries around the world propose changes to their surveillance and data collection laws, with the aim of giving cops and intelligence agencies greater powers to access people’s information. Governments already have broad digital surveillance powers and investigative tactics to solve crimes that involve encrypted data , but legislative proposals almost inevitably include provisions to expand this access even more—mandating additional logging and what amounts to backdoors or intentional flaws in encrypted products, which cryptographers and security engineers have consistently said cannot be built safely. Truly everyone who understands the issue has said it as much for decades. Yet policymakers return again and again to the idea, somehow expecting a different conclusion or a new breakthrough that will make it all possible. “There have always been some officials within certain agencies that tend to view technology as a crime scene in and of itself, and it becomes a myopic point of fixation where access is desired,” says Kate Robertson, a senior research associate at the University of Toronto’s Citizen Lab. “But that type of siloed thinking forgets that technology needs to be the secure operating platform for hospitals, for banks, for national security agencies, for police services themselves to protect victims who report private information to them.” In recent years, the UK and Australia have introduced sweeping surveillance reforms that can compel companies to break their encryption . Other encryption-threatening proposals have also emerged in the EU , France , India , Ireland , Spain , Sweden , Switzerland , and others. While not all measures have passed into law or been enacted, the hostility is clear. can broadly place requirements on tech companies, including those outside of Canada, to introduce “technical capabilities” that allow data to be accessed for law enforcement purposes. Like many such bills, C-22 says that companies will not have to introduce a “systemic vulnerability” into their systems. But opponents have pointed out that any capability to access end-to-end encrypted data amounts to a backdoor that could be discovered and abused by anyone. And this risk is only heightened even more by the ease with which anyone can now use AI tools for reverse engineering and system mapping. “Companies could be asked to introduce vulnerabilities, build backdoors, bypass, weaken or otherwise defeat encryption,” members of the US House Judiciary and Foreign Affairs committee said in a May letter to Canadian officials. In addition to potential impacts on encryption, C-22 also includes provisions that could require companies to retain metadata about user activity, something that many privacy focused services (including VPN services from Psiphon and DuckDuckGo) intentionally avoid. As a result, these companies say, they would be forced to change their business models to collect data they do not need or want to collect about their users. And researchers say that such product changes would diminish user trust while increasing the potential for widespread surveillance. “If you are asking and requiring for this infrastructural change—that they retain metadata by default—it is creating a surveillance capability within a tool that didn’t have it,” says Afsaneh Rigot, the founder of the De|Center, a research organization that aims to reduce the risk of technological harms. “There are contexts like Iran and other contexts globally, who all of this has a trickle effect on. It's not going to stay in Canada because these types of laws always get copy pasted around the world.” As more countries contemplate such laws, developers focused on privacy and anti-censorship tools are increasingly casting around for safe jurisdictions to operate in. But this still doesn’t solve the problem of reaching users in all countries around the world and for now, there are no sure bets. “Changing your headquarters isn’t much of a plan B when the law follows your users, as C-22 would,” says Joseph Lorenzo-Hall, security portfolio lead at the Internet Society. “The strongest protection is holding as little user data as possible, but ‘we don’t have it’ is no defense if governments can force you to start collecting it. A safe haven needs more than favorable winds in strong encryption. It needs laws that let companies keep their privacy promises and defend them against foreign threats to confidentiality and integrity.” Spotted something we should include next week? Let us know at [email protected] . And stay safe out there.

articles.title: Did Chinese Cars Snoop on Norway's Military?
articles.content: By Pierre-Henry Deshayes Chinese-made cars filmed sensitive information during a Norwegian military exercise, including access codes at secure sites and officials’ comings and goings, raising concerns about the risks posed by connected vehicles. Electric vehicles (EVs) by Chinese automaker Deepal, at their showroom in Kathmandu on September 13, 2024. Photo by Prakash Mathema/AFP. During a security exercise at Oslo airport on September 14-18, waiting soldiers tapping on their vehicle’s screen discovered videos recorded by the onboard cameras, the Dagens Naeringsliv (DN) newspaper revealed. The recordings showed who was getting in and out of the cars, the routes taken and even the codes used to open gates or doors to military facilities. In its report three weeks after the exercise, DN said the recordings came from rental vehicles — at least two of them Deepal brand cars, made by Chinese state-controlled automaker Changan. They were supplied to the army by Hertz Norge, which is indirectly owned by the Chinese auto group Geely. “Yes, soldiers from the Home Guard found videos from the vehicles’ sensors stored in their systems,” Lieutenant Colonel Per Gunnar Grosberghaugen, Norwegian Home Guard spokesperson, confirmed to AFP. It was not known if the recordings were shared with a third party, notably in China, but the officer could not rule out the possibility. The case highlights a paradox: while Europe’s armies are bolstering their protection against espionage and hybrid threats, the vehicles they use can collect sensitive information. Even after discovering the leaks, the military continued to use the vehicles until the end of the exercise due to a lack of alternatives and the soldiers deleted the videos, DN reported. Judging that the impact of a general ban on Chinese-made vehicles would be disproportionate to the potential security gain, the military said it preferred security procedures tailored to each site, with possible local bans on vehicles equipped with cameras and sensors regardless of their origin. Hertz Norge stressed that it complies with Norwegian and European regulations. “Our customers’ data is safe with us,” Hallvard Nerbovik, its marketing and communications director, told AFP. Embed from Getty Images “No personal data related to our rentals is shared with car manufacturers, our owners or other third parties without explicit legal grounds,” he added, without specifying whether the onboard videos may have been transferred. Changan group did not respond to AFP’s questions. Last year, tests carried out for Oslo’s Ruter public transport authority revealed that Chinese manufacturer Yutong could theoretically remotely immobilise its electric buses with their “over-the-air” update system. Norway could use the buses one day to evacuate the population in the event of an emergency. Ruter has since introduced mechanisms enabling it to monitor and delay incoming signals in order to control updates, it said. Modern vehicles are not the only potential Trojan horses. Smartwatches and fitness apps such as Strava, popular with joggers, can also expose sensitive military information. In 2018, data published by Strava made it possible to identify military sites and soldiers’ routes, notably in Afghanistan and Syria. In March, French newspaper Le Monde was able to locate the French aircraft carrier Charles de Gaulle in almost real time in the eastern Mediterranean, thanks to a sailor on board using the app. The Norwegian National Security Authority (NSM) said modern vehicles are “rolling computers that collect information”. “We don’t know for sure where the information is sent or what it’s used for,” NSM official Andreas Skjold-Lorange told AFP. The organisation, which is responsible for minimising strategic risks including digital, said that beyond the data collected, Norway should be wary of excessive dependence on a single country. Especially if that country does not cooperate with Norway on security matters. “If we become too dependent on services or products from a given country, that makes us vulnerable, whatever that country may be,” Skjold-Lorange warned. articles.title: US Border Drones: FAA Bans Civilian Flight
articles.content: Sign up now: Get ST's newsletters delivered to your inbox A footpath winds into the distance beside a section of the US-Mexico border fence constructed earlier in the day in Lochiel, Arizona, US October 8, 2026. REUTERS/Rebecca Noble/File Photo Published Oct 17, 2026, 02:55 AM Updated Oct 17, 2026, 03:15 AM Set as preferred source Listen WASHINGTON, Oct 16 - The Federal Aviation Administration said on Friday it is barring unauthorized drones along the US border with Mexico as the government steps up efforts to address concerns about illegal cross-border drug shipments. The temporary flight restriction bars any unauthorized drone activity up to 400 feet (122 m) above ground level and extends one nautical mile north of the US-Mexico border. In April, the FAA and Pentagon signed an agreement allowing the government's use of a high-energy laser counter-drone system along the southern US border with Mexico to address drone threats. The Pentagon has said there are more than 1,000 drone incursions along the US-Mexico border each month. US security officials have increasingly expressed alarm about the use of drones by Mexican cartels to drop drug packages or surveil trafficking routes. "By restricting unauthorized drone activity, we are giving commanders greater awareness, greater decision space, and more options to defend the homeland," said Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth, adding that the military "will shoot down any cartel drone that threatens America’s sovereignty.” In February, the FAA said it would halt all flights for 10 days at the El Paso, Texas, airport because of the use of the Pentagon laser system by Customs and Border Protection without completion of an FAA safety review. CBP is part of the Homeland Security Department. The FAA lifted the El Paso shutdown order after about eight hours following the White House's intervention. The US military days later shot down a CBP drone with the laser-based system, leading the FAA to expand an area in which flights were barred around Fort Hancock, Texas. DHS vowed closer communication with other agencies after the incident. Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin said on Friday that the restrictions "will help counter cartel drone threats, protect our personnel, and strengthen security in the airspace above the border." Earlier this year, media reports said drones were seen over Fort McNair in Washington where Secretary of State Marco Rubio and Hegseth live. In May, FAA Administrator Bryan Bedford told Reuters the counter-drone system is used only along southern border and is not used at Fort McNair, which is close to Reagan Washington National Airport. articles.title: IMF Warns of 'Advanced Intelligence' Risks
articles.content: By David Lawder Oct 17, 2026 Add AL-MONITOR on Google International Monetary Fund logo is seen outside the headquarters building — YURI GRIPAS By David Lawder BANGKOK, Oct 17 (Reuters) - International Monetary Fund member countries called for increasing support to countries that are facing short-term financing challenges caused by negative spillovers from wars and high energy prices, and said economic risks remain tilted to the downside. And while there has been a boost to investment and trade from "advanced intelligence technologies", they also carried risks, the chair of the International Monetary and Financial Committee said in a statement after a meeting in Bangkok. "Escalating conflicts and trade tensions could further disrupt critical trade routes, exacerbate commodity price pressures, including in refined energy products, and worsen energy and food security," said the statement issued by Saudi Finance Minister Mohammed Al-Jadaan, the chair of the IMFC. The IMFC is the main steering committee for the 191-member crisis lender. Al-Jadaan told Reuters that the language of the statement was agreed by all members. Earlier this week, the United States was pressing fellow IMF members to rename artificial intelligence as "super intelligence" in the statement, in line with US President Donald Trump's preferred name for the technology, a senior US Treasury official told Reuters. The final version of the chair's statement contained no reference to artificial intelligence. It said the uncertain impact of "advanced intelligence technologies", along with rising bond yields in major economies that spill over to highly indebted economies, "could amplify macro-financial vulnerabilities." "Rapid technological change, demographic shifts, more frequent extreme weather events and natural disasters, and geoeconomic fragmentation are compounding policy tradeoffs," the statement said. The member economies agreed to support countries that undertake reforms and address debt vulnerabilities, with specific attention to low-income and vulnerable middle-income countries and conflict-affected states. "We encourage increasing support to countries with sustainable debt and strong reform and growth enhancing agenda, but facing short-term financing challenges," the statement said, noting that several members had provided assurances of support to the IMF's Poverty Reduction and Growth Trust, which supports poor and developing countries. articles.title: Toxic AI Algorithms: Australia Demands Off-Switch
articles.content: Watch: Many social platforms already have following-only feeds - here's how they work Warning: This article contains an account of living with an eating disorder Varsha Yajman was already self-conscious about the way she looked when she joined social media as a 13-year-old. Endless workout videos making impossible promises filled her feeds. Through the screen, girls she'd never met urged her to sign up to dangerous calorie challenges. Others proudly promoted their height and weight - even the number of times they had been sent to hospital - on their profiles in a form of twisted competition. Every night as she fell asleep, Varsha would watch a stranger on the internet diarising what they'd consumed that day. "I was like, 'I don't need to eat. I can just watch other people eat'," Varsha tells the BBC. "I would find that I'd be down these really deep rabbit holes... it was like no matter how hard you tried to get out, you couldn't." Now 24 and in recovery from anorexia, Varsha says she is still served weight loss content on social media - despite having every safety setting turned on, and an exhaustive list of banned words. Image source, Tiffanie Turnbull / BBCImage caption, Varsha Yajman says social media aggravated her eating disorder It is people like her the Australian government says it is trying to protect with a new suite of laws cracking down on big tech, which were introduced to parliament this week. The centrepiece of their proposed reforms: an algorithm switch which would force social media platforms to let users turn off recommender content. The idea is that you would only see posts from accounts you follow. It isn't the first government to try this, but existing algorithm controls are often transient and come with trade-offs in app functionality. Australia has set out to make its legislation tighter to stop this. And it hopes its new laws – which would also impose a legal duty of care on online services – will help Australians become happier and healthier. But critics are concerned Prime Minister Anthony Albanese's government has bitten off more than it can chew in its fight with big tech, while others, including the Trump administration, say the reforms threaten free speech. Flynn Martin knows what it is like to be sucked into an algorithmic spiral. Self-proclaimed misogynist influencer Andrew Tate and other manosphere figures started overwhelming the then-20-year-old's social media feeds about four years ago. It was a time when Flynn, who was eventually diagnosed with bipolar disorder, was insecure, frustrated with his life and struggling with his mental health. He says he fell for the rhetoric. He soon went viral in Australia for two videos: one ranting about whether it was OK to be a straight white male, and another where he criticised a date for her frozen yoghurt order. "You find yourself in like a bit of an echo chamber... It's easy to get swept up in that," he tells the BBC. "I really bought into the idea we were living in this matrix, we had this really negative system that was designed against you. And the only way to break out of it was becoming this alpha male character." The Melbournian was only pulled from the manosphere after a period of psychosis and a hospital stay. Image source, Daniel Fermer / ABC NewsImage caption, Flynn Martin says he's still finding a healthy balance with social media Nowadays, he finds it tough to look back at that version of himself: "While there's a bit of shame and embarrassment... I think there is a bit of empathy for that younger man." Both Flynn and Varsha know social media alone isn't to blame for the worst chapter of their lives, but say it was a key factor. Countless others have stories of being confronted by social media content they didn't seek out, and didn't want to see – and there's long been suspicions the algorithms curating these platforms are harming users. Social media firms argue the potential risks are being overstated and that they already provide users with effective safety tools. But research emerging from around the world has been sketching a different picture. Studies have found social media use triggers a similar brain response to gambling and substance addiction, external; that algorithms – often unsolicited – serve up content which harms users' mental health, external, and that they're spreading disinformation and increasing polarisation, driving violence offline. Court cases and whistleblowers have aired claims that these companies know the dangers and are willing to overlook them as this technology lifts user engagement and their bottom line. "The result is that they promote content that is outrageous or that invokes strong emotions from people - so it might be anger or fear or desire or lust or insecurity, whatever it is, it's going to keep us scrolling," Chanel Contos tells the BBC. Image source, Cordelia Hsu/ReutersImage caption, Consent education campaigner Chanel Contos lobbied the government for change after founding the Teach Us Consent website in 2021 While studying the topic at university, the activist - who helped reform sexual consent education standards in Australia - came up with a campaign for change. "Fix Our Feeds" demanded recommended algorithms be turned off by default, and social media users be given the choice to opt into them. Contos envisaged a nostalgic return to the social media of the early 2010s – a time when a person's social media was filled with posts from friends or people they actually followed and their feeds were finite. More than 15,000 people signed her petition, and the campaign also won the backing of two former prime ministers, several MPs, influential figures, mental health advocates, and online safety experts. The government in September said it had listened to the Australians who had backed Contos's campaign, and announced a version of her proposal: forcing big tech to introduce an algorithm switch - but stopping short of requiring it be automatically set to off. "This is not about giving government control, it is about giving people control," Albanese said. "If people want to doom scroll… that's fine, that's up to them." Image source, Hilary Wardhaugh/Getty ImagesImage caption, Communications Minister Anika Wells (left podium) and Australian PM Anthony Albanese (right podium) announcing the upcoming Digital Duty of Care bill The policy is part of the government's Digital Duty of Care bill, which would require online services – social media firms, gaming sites, chatbots and more – to "ensure, so far as is reasonably practicable, a safe online environment". Children must be protected from "harmful" material and design features – for example, pornography and material which encourages eating disorders or harmful attitudes towards women – and adults must be protected from "seriously harmful" material and conduct, a much narrower list of illegal content. Breaches of the law could attract fines of up A$100m (£52m, $70m). "The digital duty of care answers a lot of the 'what abouts' of the social media minimum age law because it's much broader; it captures all online services and it shifts the onus of responsibility from the shoulders of victims onto the shoulders of the big tech operators who seek to make money off Australian users," Communications Minister Anika Wells told the BBC. There's been a muted response from big tech. Meta, Snap, TikTok, X and Google, which owns YouTube, have all declined BBC requests for comment, and have not made public statements about the legislation. In the days after the announcement, Instagram boss Adam Mosseri argued non-algorithmic feeds would mean users saw fewer posts from friends, and said he didn't believe his app was addictive – although a US jury recently ruled otherwise. "I think we conflate the way we colloquially use the word 'addicted' – like, 'I'm addicted to this show, and I'm binge-watching it' – and clinical addiction," he told a press briefing in Sydney. Image source, Jason Henry/Bloomberg via Getty ImagesImage caption, Instagram chief Adam Mosseri argues recommender algorithms are essential to user enjoyment Right-wing parties in Australia – and the Trump administration – have said the algorithms proposal and the broader bill both risk forcing over-moderation and censorship. But those who defend the law say that won't happen because you can still follow who you want and share what you want. "If adults listen to manosphere podcasts, or people post their views about the government, or make memes, or want to say the moon landing was fake – they can continue to do so without restriction," Wells said this week. The proposal seems to be far less divisive amongst the public and online safety experts compared with Australia's social media ban for children. However, the big question is: how will Australia implement this policy when, so far, it has been struggling to implement the ban? Surveys suggest most children who were on social media before the ban still are, and no fines have been issued. Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption, Australian regulators are investigating potential breaches of the social media ban The EU's attempt at introducing algorithm controls in 2023 – after which platforms rolled out following-only feeds – is a cautionary tale. Social media firms have indicated the take-up of safety and control features like this has been low and cite it as evidence users like their products the way they are. Experts say there is a reason for that. "Platforms do what the law orders, but in such a clunky way that users don't actually enjoy the option and stick with the default, algorithmic experience," researcher Chris Zomer, from the ARC Centre of Excellence for the Digital Child, wrote in The Conversation, external. On Instagram for example, when you turn off the algorithm, you can't see direct messages or access your profile and settings. When you leave the app, it reverts back to an algorithm-governed feed on your return. The only place where these issues don't exist is the Netherlands. It was changed there after a Dutch court last year found Meta in breach of the EU's Digital Services Act. Image source, Benjamin Fanjoy/Bloomberg via Getty ImagesImage caption, Meta lost an appeal against the Dutch court's ruling in March, meaning users in the Netherlands retain choice over their home feeds The rules for Australia aren't set in stone yet, but the government says following-only feeds must not be harder to use or less functional, that algorithm settings must be "obvious", and that they must not change without an "explicit choice" by the user, even if they leave the app. Buoyed by her success in Australia, Contos is now taking her campaign global. "We feel like Canada, UK, Australia are all very aligned on online safety... Then if those three jurisdictions are doing it, it could become a critical mass thing." Though experiences like theirs helped inspire these reforms, both Flynn and Varsha are somewhat sceptical of them. Varsha says she struggles to believe a country like Australia can outmuscle big tech: so she's not sure the Digital Duty of Care bill will work. And Flynn says lawmakers should be "realistic" about the potential of the algorithm switch: "At the end of the day we use social media as a form of entertainment." Polling earlier this month indicated two-thirds of their fellow Gen-Zs would keep their social media algorithms – though nearly half of Australians more generally would turn theirs off. Though Varsha admits she is unlikely to make much use of an algorithm switch, she appreciates having the choice. "On a bad day I'm still susceptible to all of the things that I was at 17. To know that, if I'm having a bad day, I can opt out makes me feel really good." If you've been affected by the issues raised in this story, you could speak to a health professional or an organisation that offers support. Details of organisations offering advice and support for people in the UK are available from BBC Action Line.

articles.title: Nextgov: Tech Bills Target Flock, Data Centers
articles.content: Stay Connected Featured eBooks Health Technology: Relaunch of VA EHR Read Now Law Enforcement Technology Read Now Insights & Reports By Edward Graham , Managing Editor, Nextgov/FCW | October 16, 2026 05:25 PM ET Lawmakers are continuing to take bipartisan aim at the use of artificial intelligence-powered surveillance systems and at data center development and operations. Tech Bills of the Week Stopping federal funds from going to AI-powered surveillance cameras Rep. Rashida Tlaib, D-Mich., introduced legislation on Wednesday that would prohibit federal funds from being used to purchase or operate any automated mass surveillance systems, including AI-powered cameras provided by Flock. In a press release, the congresswoman’s office said her proposal — the Get the Flock Out of Our Communities Act — “is the only bill in Congress designed to completely prohibit the use of automated mass surveillance technology, including biometric surveillance systems and facial recognition technology.” Sen. Josh Hawley, R-Mo., introduced a separate measure late last month that would impose data guardrails on the use of the surveillance systems. Rep. Pat Harrigan, R-N.C., also introduced a measure on Thursday that would “restrict the usage of automated license plate reader system by governmental entities,” although a public version of that bill’s text is not yet available. “Flock’s technology isn’t making us safer,” Tlaib said in a statement. “Instead it has been used to stalk people, mis-identify and arrest innocent people, surveil protestors, and wrongfully record our neighbors. My bill would prevent our government on all levels from selling us out to Big Tech companies that trample our civil rights for profit.” Making data centers pay for their power usage Rep. Eugene Vindman, D-Va., introduced a measure on Wednesday that seeks to keep communities from having to foot the bill for data centers’ power expenses by requiring large and medium-sized data centers “to pay the full incremental costs associated with their electricity use.” The bill would apply to data centers and high-density computing facilities that have electricity demands of at least 20 megawatts. “As data centers and artificial intelligence drive growing demand for electricity, we need to make sure the companies benefiting from that growth pay their fair share,” Vindman said in a statement. Removing tax breaks for data centers Sen. Bernie Moreno, R-Ohio, also introduced legislation on Thursday that would prohibit data centers from receiving federal and state incentives for their development or operations. Details of Moreno’s measure, known as the Recapturing Excessive Corporate Largesse through Accountability and Incentive Measures — or RECLAIM — Act, were first reported by Politico. The outlet said the senator’s bill includes a provision stating that “States and political subdivisions thereof should promptly repeal or reform any tax incentive programs that are specific to data centers.” Mandating disclosure of AI use in political ads Rep. Yvette Clarke, D-N.Y., reintroduced legislation on Thursday that would require political advertisements to include a disclaimer if they include any artificial intelligence-generated photos or video. Clarke first rolled out the measure in July 2023 and told Nextgov/FCW at the time that “for those who want to be deceptive or to harm their opponents, they can easily do some real damage with AI-generated advertising.” The congresswoman’s bill calls for relevant ads “to include a statement within the contents of the advertisements if generative AI was used to generate any image or video footage in the advertisements.” In a press release, Clarke said that “if AI content can manipulate and deceive people on a large scale, it can be a serious threat to our democracy and have devastating consequences for our national and election security.” Creating a new federal platform to combat elder scams Reps. Marie Gluesenkamp Perez, D-Wash., and Tom Barrett, R-Mich., rolled out legislation on Thursday that looks to crack down on fraud and scams targeting elderly Americans by creating a new website and 24/7 reporting hotline. The measure looks to address the often fragmented fraud reporting system across government by creating a streamlined reporting and assistance process. The lawmakers said their bill would create a reporting platform similar to the one that the Department of Veterans Affairs created in 2024 to combat scams targeting retired servicemembers. Barrett chairs the House Veterans’ Affairs Technology Modernization Subcommittee. “Families need resources to recognize and quickly report suspected fraud,” Barrett said in a statement. “By establishing a 24/7, one-stop shop for addressing elder fraud, this bipartisan bill will protect vulnerable seniors and empower law enforcement to crack down on these criminals.” Share This:

articles.title: Why Companies May Be Liable for AI Errors
articles.content: Artificial intelligence has moved quickly from a novelty on the job to a common workplace tool. Gallup found that 52% of U.S. employees and 68% of professional services workers were using AI by February 2026. Thomson Reuters similarly found in spring 2026 that 74% of professionals use AI several times a week for work. This widespread use shouldn’t surprise anyone. For accountants, attorneys, consultants, and other professionals, AI can accelerate research, summarize complex information, and assist with writing and other forms of communication. But its rapid adoption has a big downside—AI can produce information that sounds authoritative and looks polished while being completely wrong . And when AI generates mistakes, responsibility for those errors belongs to the professional or business relying on the AI output—not companies that develop AI systems. AI errors have led to lawsuits, court fines, financial consequences and public embarrassment from fabricated citations, nonexistent sources, and inaccurate AI-generated information. These cases raise an increasingly important question: How can professionals benefit from AI without outsourcing the judgment their work requires? We are two certified public accountants who research tax accounting . In the September 2026 issue of Journal of Accountancy, we examined what happened in Clinco v. Commissioner , a case before the U.S. Tax Court where an attorney submitted a brief to the court with allegedly fake citations. The Tax Court is a specialized federal court that resolves disputes between taxpayers and the IRS. This case involved a restaurant owner accused of underreporting more than US$2 million in business receipts and claiming unsupported depreciation deductions on rental properties. The main issue concerned Clinco’s accounting records used to determine how much of their income to tax. The taxpayers’ attorney, Abraham Wagner, cited four cases to support his argument that an IRS notice assessing additional taxes was invalid. The court determined that three of the citations appeared to be AI-generated hallucinations that cited nonexistent Tax Court cases. The court rejected the taxpayer’s argument and warned Wagner that submitting fake citations could lead to sanctions from the court, including financial penalties or disciplinary action against Wagner. Ultimately, the court did not sanction Wagner in the case, but the decision stands to put attorneys and other professionals in Tax Court on notice that AI hallucinations will not be tolerated. AI errors made on behalf of clients are not limited to briefs drafted by attorneys. Nor are these mishaps limited to the United States. When Deloitte produced a 237-page report in 2025 for the Australian government examining its automated system for penalizing welfare recipients who failed to meet job-seeking requirements, it contained nonexistent academic citations and a fabricated quotation it attributed to a federal court judgment. The global consulting firm later issued a revised version of the error-ridden report. Deloitte blamed generative AI for the errors in the original and agreed to partially refund its fees. Like most airlines, Air Canada has a chatbot on its website to respond to its customers’ questions. The chatbot told a customer in November 2022 that he could buy a plane ticket under a bereavement policy and be reimbursed later. This was not company policy, and Air Canada refused to honor what the chatbot had told the customer. The customer sued the airline and won 812 Canadian dollars in damages. The British Columbia Civil Resolution Tribunal ruled that Air Canada had failed to take reasonable care to ensure that its AI bot provided accurate information and agreed with the customer that the airline had negligently misrepresented the bereavement policy. There have been other lawsuits filed against AI platforms and providers. In 2025, for example, a Georgia court dismissed a defamation lawsuit against OpenAI after its ChatGPT tool falsely accused Mark Walters, a radio host, of embezzlement. The court ruled in favor of summary judgment for OpenAI and found Walters had not established fault and damages. There is also an ongoing case, Keene v. Google LLC , that is similar to the Walters case. Keene, a TV producer, sued after Google’s AI summaries allegedly published false information about Keene’s criminal history. In September 2026, the court ruled that some of his defamation claims may proceed, without deciding yet whether Google was liable. Unfortunately, for anyone using AI to save time and use less labor, AI errors are often hard to spot. Unlike most obvious mistakes humans make, an AI-generated error may include supporting explanations, citations or references that make a passage appear complete and credible. The National Institute of Standards and Technology issued a report on AI risk management in July 2024 that calls AI mistakes and hallucinations “confabulations”—the confident presentation of erroneous or false information. Some researchers draw a more specific distinction between hallucinations, in which AI invents information outright, and confabulations, in which it fills gaps or distorts real information in a plausible way. Either kind of problem can be hard to detect without independent verification, but confabulations mimic actual research so closely they can trick AI users into believing the AI output is valid. A 2024 Stanford University study of specialized AI tools for legal research found erroneous results in 17% to 33% of the responses tested. Yet those findings and other grounds for concern about accuracy have not stopped many law firms from embracing AI tools due to their potential to save time and improve efficiency. Recent surveys indicate law firms and other employers have not adopted enough workplace safeguards to spot and root out AI-generated mistakes. A 2026 survey by the Nationwide insurance company found that only 36% of surveyed businesses have written AI policies, and only 37% provide any training on responsible AI use. As AI becomes more and more common in the workplace, we believe it’s clear that telling employees simply to “check the AI” is not enough. Businesses and the people working for them need clear expectations about when it’s appropriate to use AI, which outputs require independent verification, and who is ultimately responsible for the final work. AI may change how professional work gets done, but it does not change where the buck stops. Sarah Webber is an associate professor of accounting at the University of Dayton . articles.title: NASSCOM Urges Review of AI Procurement for Gov't
articles.content: Access a copy of the parliamentary report here: [ pdf ] The industry body, the National Association of Software and Service Companies (NASSCOM), has urged the government to review its public procurement processes to give domestic AI foundation models preferential treatment against global Big Tech giants like Google and Meta. This was revealed in the 17th report of the Committee on External Affairs, titled “India’s Role in Global Tech Diplomacy, Digital Governance, Outer Space Diplomacy, AI and Emerging Innovations,” tabled in September 2026. NASSCOM is a trade association representing over 3,500 member companies, including IT firms such as Tata Consultancy Services (TCS), Cognizant and Accenture India, as well as global capability centres (GCCs) and startups. The full list can be explored here . NASSCOM acknowledged the government’s investments in AI but warned that these efforts could be undermined without a clear pathway for adopting domestic AI models if local startups are forced to compete purely on price with global Big Tech models. NASSCOM highlighted the following issues: The lowest-bidder tender trap and Big Tech’s competitive advantage: During its oral submission before the committee, NASSCOM highlighted the procurement process of AI services that could disadvantage government-funded AI developers such as Sarvam AI: “We do not have an AI inclusion roadmap right now… We are investing in foundational companies like Sarvam AI and BharatGen, who are building India’s AI models, but we are not talking about how they will get consumed by Indians. Government procurement for these models still has to follow the L1 [lowest bidder] tender process.” – Parliamentary Report NASSCOM cites China’s protected AI market to support domestic developers: NASSCOM’s submission drew a comparison with China’s approach, where its government apparently created a protected domestic market for its homegrown AI models, allowing them to grow and compete against global Big Tech. “China gave real preference to its own companies for their models to be adopted; if we still compete purely on price with Meta and Google and others, who have spent hundreds of billions of dollars, we will never have a level playing field. We need to look at our procurement processes to ensure that what we are investing in gets some disproportionate preference.” –  Parliamentary Report The Mercator Institute for China Studies (MERICS), a European think tank, argued in a research paper that the “protected home market” of China has helped large language model (LLM) developers like DeepSeek, as well as the AI ecosystem, including the semiconductor and AI chip industries. The Committee’s Recommendations: While the parliamentary committee did not explicitly recommend amending the General Financial Rules governing procurement and the L1 (lowest bidder) tender process, it strongly acknowledged the structural bottleneck highlighted by NASSCOM. “The Committee are concerned that India still lacks several of the basic foundations that would make it a genuine AI power…The Committee are of the view that the gap between India’s demonstrated capability and its realised leadership is not primarily a gap of resources or talent, but of follow-through, adoption pathways, strategic clarity, and the pace at which these foundations are being built. The Government should ensure that the opportunity AI presents for India’s development is not left to be realised by default, but is pursued as deliberately.” What are the companies under the IndiaAI mission? In March 2024, the Indian government approved an outlay of Rs 10,371.92 crore for the IndiaAI Mission. As MediaNama reported then, this budget was supposed to be used for building “programs and partnerships across the public and private sectors.” However, according to a parliamentary reply on IndiaAI Mission fund releases, the government reported the following figures as of February 9, 2026: 2026–27: It has not released any funds yet, against a budget estimate (BE) of Rs 1,000 crore. 2024–25: It released Rs 21.79 crore, against a revised estimate (RE) of Rs 173 crore. 2025–26: It released Rs 379.15 crore, against an RE of Rs 800 crore. These include activities like:  Providing compute capacity Developing and deploying indigenous large multimodal models (LMMs) Streamlining access to quality non-personal datasets for AI innovation Development of AI apps and AI-based solutions Increasing accessibility to AI programs and courses Financing deep-tech AI startups Implementing responsible AI projects for “trust and safety” The report identifies the following 12 companies and initiatives selected under the IndiaAI Mission:  Sarvam AI, Soket AI, Gnani AI, Gan AI, Avatar AI, GenLoop, Zentieq, Intellihealth, Shodh AI, Fractal Analytics Ltd., Tech Mahindra Maker’s Lab IIT Bombay-led BharatGen initiative (as an academic consortium) In October 2026, MeitY released a tender document seeking AI computing capacity of over 10,000 GPUs for “ministries, departments, academia, research institutions, startups and industry.” Read MediaNama’s breakdown of the Request for Empanelment (RFE) proposal here . articles.title: AI Isn't Ready for Convoluted Genomes
articles.content: Save Story Save this story Save Story Save this story of this story appeared in Quanta Magazine . structure was deduced in the 1950s, DNA has been hailed by many biologists as the secret of life. They’ve read and studied the information stored in the DNA found in the cells of living organisms, known as their genomes , and claimed that this genetic database must be some kind of blueprint, code script, or computer. But if DNA really does harbor some greater secret about how life works, biologists have yet to find it. In fact, the human genome is less a script than a puzzle that gets harder the closer they look. Knowing the entire sequence —the order of all 3 billion or so of our DNA’s chemical building blocks, nearly fully deduced by the international Human Genome Project between 1990 and 2003—hasn’t helped much. That investigation showed that barely 2 percent of the human genome consists of actual genes, the information-coding sequences of DNA. It’s now clear that understanding the human genome is no longer a matter of figuring out what each gene does. The deeper and much harder question is how those genes are used , or regulated, a question that seems to involve some and perhaps much of the rest of the genome. By switching suites of genes on and off, the many different cell types in our bodies can all be created from the same material. Cells also regulate their genes from moment to moment in response to a constant inflow of signals from their neighbors and surroundings. But the processes that govern gene regulation are proving so complex that some biologists wonder whether a full understanding of it—of how the genome really works—will ever be within the grasp of our puny minds. Some are counting on outsourcing the analysis to artificial intelligence. Genomic “foundation models” such as Evo 2, Genos, and Google DeepMind’s AlphaGenome are trained on vast quantities of genomic data , which biologists use to make predictions about how differences in DNA sequence affect biological processes and ultimately the traits (including disease risk) of a whole organism. These algorithms don’t worry about the complicated regulatory stuff going on. All of that is supposedly subsumed by the algorithm’s “training,” through which it deduces correlations from cases we already know about. Courtesy of Quanta This approach is likely to be useful, but for those who crave real understanding of how the genome, and ultimately life itself, works, a computational black box will never suffice. And perhaps more to the point, the genome might not submit to the kind of straightforward input-output approach that such AI models ultimately assume. That’s because the genome is no blueprint or algorithm. It’s something else. the product of around 4 billion years of evolution , perhaps it’s not surprising that our genome is complicated. The surprise has been what those complications are. “Our genome is not what we might make it if we sat down at the drawing board,” said the biologist Karen Adelman, who studies gene regulation at Harvard Medical School. Making a protein from its gene is a two-stage affair. First the DNA is read, letter by letter, by an enzyme called a polymerase, which creates a copy of that code in a related molecule called messenger RNA (mRNA). This is called transcription. The mRNA is then read by a piece of molecular machinery called the ribosome, which constructs the protein—a process called translation. The proteins made by the ribosome then go off to do their jobs in making and sustaining the organism. This picture is still more or less correct. But it turns out that “the genes are probably not the most interesting part of the genome,” Adelman said. What matters more is how our genes, many of which we share with simpler organisms, are regulated—turned on and off. Which proteins a cell needs changes over time and according to cell type: muscle, brain, skin, and so on. How the genes that encode those proteins are regulated depends on some of the genome that doesn’t code for proteins. Biologists have known about gene regulation, and the involvement of “noncoding” DNA, since the 1960s. But for many years, most of what they understood about this came from studies of simple organisms like bacteria , where the principles are generally straightforward. It has gradually become clear, though, that in complex eukaryotic organisms like us, gene regulation is far more complicated, involving overlapping systems of oversight and control, each with its own intricacies. Courtesy of Quanta Transcription gets started by proteins called transcription factors, which are like the operations managers of gene regulation. These proteins stick to sections of DNA (typically close to the target gene) and recruit the polymerase enzyme to make an mRNA copy. In bacteria, transcription factors are rather like keys that fit the locks of unique binding sites on DNA. But that’s not how they work in complex organisms. In us, the logic of transcription factors is more difficult to parse. For one thing, our transcription factors don’t show strong preferences for particular DNA binding sites. What’s more, they tend to work in pairs or groups. And a given transcription factor might have different effects in different contexts, such as activating gene transcription in one cell type but suppressing it in another, depending on which other transcription factors are around. that. But in the human genome the logic is more like what computer scientists designate “AND.” Many signals are integrated to reach a regulatory decision: This and that and also that other thing. In this case, regulation can be more responsive to nuances of context, and the regulatory knobs are tunable rather than being just on or off . “This is part of the beauty” of our regulatory complexity, Adelman said. Courtesy of Quanta When they interact with the genome, transcription factors bind to pieces of DNA called enhancers—which present a puzzle of their own. Enhancers are gathering points for transcription factors, and they are thought to be the decisive influence on transcription: They deliver the “go” signal for a waiting polymerase to make an mRNA version of the DNA sequence. Seems simple enough, but mapping enhancers to their respective genes is far from straightforward. Our genome has hundreds of thousands, perhaps millions, of enhancers. That means we have many more of them than we have genes. Each gene might be influenced by many enhancers, and each enhancer might influence multiple genes. “It’s embarrassing that 25 years after the Human Genome Project , we don’t know where all the enhancers are in the genome, let alone what they do when they act and which genes they control,” said Wendy Bickmore, a genome biologist at the University of Edinburgh. Biologists do know that most enhancers won’t respond to a single transcription factor. Their activation “requires a cocktail,” Bickmore said. “That’s what gives [an enhancer] that exquisite specificity—because it’s only in a particular cell at a particular time that you have the right combination of factors to bind and activate that enhancer.” The existence of such so-called “distal” enhancers “seems bonkers,” Bickmore said. “How do you get that information from over there to over here, to the gene that needs to be activated? That’s a largely unanswered question.” One of the answers comes in the form of a loop. Distal enhancers are brought to the gene they regulate on great loops of DNA or, more strictly, of chromatin, the combination of DNA and its packaging proteins that are unraveled as if from a ball of wool. The loops are created by a protein motor called cohesin, which runs up and down the DNA strand and extrudes it as needed. Once cohesin has formed a loop to bring elements together, what then? It was once thought that they then stick together or assemble into a molecular machine, but they don’t. Rather, the components appear to form a loose but dense blob in which they interact rather weakly, fleetingly, and indiscriminately—a sort of committee, sometimes called a condensate. Courtesy of Quanta These transcription hubs are extremely fluid and differ from one cell to another. “There’ll be a bit of loop extrusion going on over here, in the next cell it might be over here, and the whole thing is turning over incredibly fast,” Bickmore said. Even if the cells are notionally identical—both skin cells, say—exactly what the gene-regulatory machinery is up to at any moment is never quite the same in any two of them. Chromatin loops are just one reason why a gene’s transcription depends on the shape and structure of the chromatin around it. of a chromosome—one of the 46 units into which our genomes are divided—is of a compact, X-shaped cluster of chromatin . But any time a cell is not actively dividing, its chromatin is unwound into what looks like a tangled mess. There is order to the chaos, however. Some parts of chromatin are densely packed into a form called heterochromatin. The compacted DNA there is relatively inaccessible to transcription factors; the genes it contains are typically silenced. Meanwhile, other parts are relatively loose, open, and accessible: This is called euchromatin. Courtesy of Quanta One aspect of this 3D organization is the clustering of segments of chromatin into compartments called topologically associating domains (TADs). Within a TAD, the genes seem to be coregulated: switched on or off in groups. Such groups keep suites of genes active or silent together to form and provide function in different cell types. Cohesin is also involved in the shuffling of chromatin to construct TADs—a dynamic process in which the chromatin is constantly rearranged in our cells. or stuck directly to DNA. Some of these epigenetic modifications can alter the electrical charges on histones, which changes how the proteins attract or repel one another and so rejigs the chromatin packing. Epigenetic modifications to chromatin are like annotations of the DNA script that change its meaning in a given context. When cells divide, the epigenetic annotations are copied, too. How and when the marks get added and changed, and what each type of mark means for gene activity, are complex questions with no simple answers. Some researchers talk of an “epigenetic code” governing this aspect of gene regulation, but it’s far from clear if anything so systematic really exists. All of these processes and others can determine whether a gene gets transcribed into mRNA. But there are further layers of regulation that determine whether the mRNA is then translated into a corresponding protein—and which protein arises. Courtesy of Quanta This post-transcriptional regulation is often controlled by RNA molecules that are said to be noncoding. These short-lived molecules aren’t templates for proteins, as mRNA is, but have other jobs of their own. While mRNA is produced from the protein-coding areas of DNA (so-called “coding genes”), noncoding RNAs are transcribed from other DNA regions now generally described as noncoding genes. These noncoding RNAs are versatile , taking on varied roles in a cell. Researchers are learning more about what they can do every day, and many if not most of them seem to be involved in gene regulation. Small noncoding RNAs called microRNAs, for example, can silence mRNAs before they can be translated into proteins. They do this by guiding special enzymes to a particular mRNA to degrade or chemically modify it. The microRNAs don’t do this job alone but, not unlike transcription factors, act combinatorially, in groups, and in a rather promiscuous manner: A given microRNA might regulate many mRNAs, and a given mRNA might be regulated by many microRNAs. . In this way, the workings of the genome are less like a program’s inevitable progression and more like an adaptive and responsive process. Another post-transcriptional complication is that mRNAs get translated to protein only after they have been reorganized. Fresh from transcription, an mRNA contains sequences that encode bits of protein, called exons, as well as sequences that shouldn’t be translated and need to be snipped out, called introns. (Strictly speaking, this pre-edited RNA is called pre-mRNA.) The job of editing introns out and splicing exons together is done by a molecular assembly called the spliceosome, which is made from several proteins together with various noncoding RNAs. Courtesy of Quanta The spliceosome too can be sensitive to context, so that it might splice the pre-mRNA to encode one protein in one cell type and a slightly different protein in another. Sometimes these different protein “isoforms” can have very different roles. Transcription factors, for example, are often alternatively spliced in this way, and their isoforms can take on different regulatory tasks —some might activate gene expression, for instance, while others repress it. All told, these and other regulatory mechanisms show that the genome is far from some automated program running in the background to build us and keep us alive. Our cells are, in effect, making complex decisions about how to use their genes—both the information they contain and the structure they assume. Thus, cells need to assemble a rather loose and fuzzy committee of components, such as transcription factors and enhancers, to get transcription underway, which also depends on how the chromatin strand is shaped and molded at that moment. Then there are further layers of decisionmaking and action-taking in between mRNA and the final, functional protein. Courtesy of Quanta And for that reason, not at all easy to understand. “I wouldn’t have designed it this way if I was God,” Bickmore said. “But here we are!” Why is gene regulation in animals like us so darned complicated? One potential answer is that evolution doesn’t have the foresight to design with efficiency and transparent logic, but merely tinkers with what it has already available. Maybe so—but eukaryotic gene regulation isn’t just a messy version of what happens in bacteria. It has different principles, and there’s surely a reason for them. and of genome organization might have been the only means of generating complexity in the organism. For example, organisms with many tissue types and varied lifestyles required more control over which genes were on or off in a given cell. One thing this demanded was more and more noncoding regulatory sequences in DNA. But then they couldn’t all fit close to the gene itself. “As you get more complexity, you need to add more and more enhancers,” Bickmore said. “But where are you going to put them? You start to put them farther and farther away. Once they are [far enough], you start to need TADs and three-dimensional [chromatin] folding to allow those things to work.” We also need regulatory complexity because, over evolutionary time, the human genome has accumulated DNA from parasitic viruses in the form of jumping genetic material called transposable elements . These sequences have inserted themselves all over our chromosomes and are good at replicating themselves. To sift the good DNA from the bad, we needed additional layers of regulation to ensure that cells weren’t translating RNAs they don’t really need or that could be actively harmful. With so many context-dependent checks and balances in the workings of our genome, it is evidently not a program or algorithm that predictably generates the same outcome in every situation. It’s an open informational system that responds to external inputs and the genome’s dynamic internal conditions. This poses a challenge if AI relies solely on the genetic sequences within genomes to predict what genomes will do . genomic foundation models, such as AlphaGenome, hope that all these layers of regulation—transcription factors, splicing, epigenetic marks, loops, chromatin packing, and so on—will be implicitly included in the correlations that the algorithms learn between genetic sequence and organismal traits. They’re content for the complexity described above to be in a black box, so long as the model generates accurate predictions . But will that work? Fundamentally, the challenge is that the genome is not a set of static, linear instructions. It is highly dynamic, and it uses its information contextually, with combinatorial and promiscuous logic. “Whether we’ll ever be able to capture that aspect” in algorithms like AlphaGenome, “I don’t know,” she said. Yet the problem goes even deeper because the functioning of specific organisms, including each of us, doesn’t just depend on genomes. Other factors, such as diet, environment, microbiome , and, for us at least, culture, can matter hugely, too—not just in terms of how we act and how healthy we are but also in the state of our genome itself. The biologist Adrian Woolfson, cofounder of California-based biotech company Genyro, which aims to use AI systems for so-called “generative biology,” calls this information cloud the “informiome.” Courtesy of Quanta “While the human genome forms the foundation of the human informiome, other layers of extra-genetic information are equally important,” Woolfson wrote in his book On the Future of Species , published in April 2026. Genomic foundation models won’t even be able to predict all the consequences of genetic mutations, he argued, because the relevant information is not in the genome sequence in the first place. So how should we think about the genome? Maybe the only metaphors that can capture the way the genome really works must come from biology itself. In 2020, the biological historian Evelyn Fox compared the genome to “an exquisitely sensitive reactive system.” Rather than a sequence of genes leading to the formation of traits, she said, it’s more of “a device for regulating the production of specific proteins in response to constantly changing signals it receives from its environment.” upon being awarded the 1983 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine for her discovery of transposons. The genome, she declared, is “a highly sensitive organ of the cell, monitoring genomic activities and correcting common errors, sensing the unusual and unexpected events and responding to them, often by restructuring the genome.” Research since that time has fleshed out this image, revealing how the shape of chromatin can matter as much as the information its DNA sequences encode and how an army of molecules collaborates to reorganize it and make collective decisions about how to use its genetic information in context-dependent ways. There is no human technology that works this way, so metaphors such as blueprints, programs, or computers will always fall short. Bickmore is optimistic that the workings of the genome are understandable, despite its complexity. “We’ve got a handle on it now,” she said. “We might not know the details, but I think the whole field is coalescing now into a framework where we’re thinking along similar lines.” AI can surely help with this sense-making, but in the end, human reasoning will be needed to discern the fundamental principles. “McClintock was far more on point than people realized at the time,” Adelman said. “What she said was that the genome isn’t static—it’s living.” Original story reprinted with permission from Quanta Magazine , an editorially independent publication of the Simons Foundation whose mission is to enhance public understanding of science by covering research developments and trends in mathematics and the physical and life sciences.

articles.title: BAE Systems Cyber Incident Disrupts US Bankruptcy Courts
articles.content: A cybersecurity incident at BAE Systems has halted the production and delivery of bankruptcy notices for every federal bankruptcy court in the United States, disrupting a core administrative function of the judiciary with no announced date for restoration. The Bankruptcy Noticing Center, known as the BNC, produces and transmits notices in bankruptcy cases nationwide. BAE Systems, a defense contractor, operates the center’s systems and websites on behalf of the federal judiciary. In a statement published Thursday , the Administrative Office of the U.S. Courts said the incident affected BAE’s information technology and the websites supporting the center’s operations.  The office said BAE is investigating and working to restore operations.  “We are aware of a security incident that is isolated to the BNC system and have taken immediate steps to address it,” a BAE Systems spokesperson told CyberScoop. “No other systems have been affected.”  The disruption has taken the center’s websites offline, including bnc.uscourts.gov, bankruptcynotices.uscourts.gov and notices.uscourts.gov, along with the National Creditor Registration Service. It has stopped the production and distribution of notices, paper and electronic, since Oct. 9.  As of Friday, those websites were still offline.  Notices of the incident first started this week when a note was posted Tuesday on the U.S. Bankruptcy court website, calling it a “nationwide service interruption” with no mention of cyberactivity. The Administrative Office’s Oct. 15 statement was the first to use the words cybersecurity incident.  Neither announcement identified a cause, said whether information was accessed, or gave an estimate for restoration. Clerk of Court Joe Falzone said in the announcement that courts are still taking new filings, opening cases and processing paperwork. People who need to serve documents can look up creditor and party addresses by running searches in the courts’ electronic filing system, then compare the two lists to make sure nothing is missing. But the notice warned that those lists might not include addresses that people registered through the BNC’s Electronic Bankruptcy Noticing program or the National Creditor Registration Service. Some people who are supposed to receive notice might not appear in the records. The incident would mark the second in as many years to affect U.S. Courts. In 2025, there was a major breach of the federal judiciary’s electronic case filing system.  The Administrative Office said it has been in communication with the affected courts as BAE Systems continues its investigation.  UPDATE, 10/16/2026, 1:45 p.m.: This story has been updated with comment from BAE Systems.

articles.title: Brave Browser Introduces Encrypted AI Chat for Privacy
articles.content: Browser maker using trusted hardware to protect conversations with GLM 5.3 Flash Thomas Claburn Thomas Claburn AI AND SOFTWARE REPORTER Published fri 16 Oct 2026 // 13:15 UTC Make us preferred on Google Benchmarked: Nvidia's RTX Spark notebook delivers serious local AI compute, at a price 1 day ago $24,000 AI experiment ports TypeScript compiler to Rust 2 days ago TSMC sends scouts to check whether America's datacenters can deliver 2 days ago Linux kernel devs drop obligatory confession of AI tool usage 3 days ago Researchers cig-nal their faith in AI by taking up smoking 3 days ago Brave Software has set up a secure space so those using its browser can converse with the company's AI assistant in private. At a time when AI agents like Meta's Muse ask for extensive access to personal information, and AI companies repurpose conversations for training , this amounts to swimming against the tide. Following up on an experiment launched last November to implement a confidential channel for LLM conversations with the help of NEAR AI's trusted execution environment (TEE), the browser maker has connected its Leo AI assistant to Z.ai 's GLM 5.3 Flash under the protection of end-to-end encryption. The result is that Brave users can submit a prompt to Leo that gets encrypted on-device and sent over the network using Oblivious HTTP , a protocol for separating network requests from associated content. Brave's AI Gateway forwards the encrypted query to the TEE without passing along the user's IP address. After Brave verifies the enclave's attestation, the browser encrypts the query using a key bound to the TEE. The TEE decrypts the request, runs it through the AI model, and sends back an encrypted response that gets decrypted by the receiving browser. "In 2014, I argued in ' Trust but Verify ' that users shouldn't have to place blind trust in the software they rely on," said Brendan Eich, co-founder and CEO of Brave, in a statement . "They should be able to verify it; this is a user-first principle. AI has raised the stakes, yet too much of it still runs on 'trust me bro' promises, often at the user's expense." NEAR AI's confidential AI pipeline is built with Intel TDX and Nvidia Confidential Compute. It includes end-to-end encryption that keeps Brave from knowing what was asked and NEAR AI from knowing who did the asking during the network hop. Data isolation prevents the prompt or response from being read during processing. Responses are signed in the TEE and there's attestation so users can confirm there's no model bait-and-switch . Leo's GLM 5.3 Flash brain may be isolated in this scenario, but Brave's AI bot can still conduct searches from within the TEE via the Brave Search API's LLM context endpoint. And any searches done this way transit via the TEE rather than the user's browser, which keeps the user's IP address out of the picture. The implementation isn't quite complete: Brave intends to work on moving the verification step into the browser and to publish a log of TEE keys, and to provide enclave attestation for exact model weights loaded into memory, among other things. Brave is not the only company trying to make AI less of a data exposure risk. Apple , AWS , Google , Nvidia , and Microsoft all have some form of private cloud compute infrastructure for AI.  Then there's Prem AI , which promises encrypted inference, not to mention providers advertising zero data retention, which isn't as verifiable. One way to ensure privacy while using AI is to run inference on local hardware using an open weight model, assuming the model and the machine running it haven't been compromised. ® ai ai and ml end-to-end encryption confidential computing Make us preferred on Google

articles.title: Kim Jong Un's Luxury Boat Spotted Near Summer Retreat
articles.content: Image source, Vantor/BBCBySoram Cheon, BBC Korean and Aghnia Adzkia, East Asia Visual JournalismAn 80m (263ft) luxury vessel has been repeatedly spotted in satellite images off North Korea's Wonsan coast from July to mid-October this year. What stands out is the 50m swimming pool along the deck, with a cluster of waterslides at one end. After sitting idle for months at a maintenance facility, it relocated in early July to waters off a strip of coastline known as the Kalma Peninsula. This is close to Wonsan, a seaside resort with a sprawling villa used by North Korean leader Kim Jong Un and his family. It was not the only large vessel on the move. A handful of others were also repeatedly seen near Kim's villa, in satellite images analysed by the BBC. The vessels are widely believed to be used by Kim and his family. Former North Korean officials, defectors and experts say it would be difficult for anyone unconnected to the regime's leadership to own or freely use vessels of this size. "In winter, they would keep them at the shipyard. When summer came, they would bring them out and move them to Kim Jong Un's villa or towards Kalma, and use them for swimming and recreation," says Ri Jong Ho. Ri was once an official at the Workers' Party's Office 39, which is believed to be involved in raising and managing foreign currency for the leadership. The wealth of those who sit at the top of the secretive North Korean dictatorship is just as hard to pin down as the country's economic figures. The United Nations and others rely on estimates to classify North Korea as one of the world's poorest countries, with an especially large military budget that funds a sanctioned nuclear programme. Most North Koreans, according to a 2025 UN report, live under "systematic, widespread and gross human rights violations" with total state control, widespread forced labour, and chronic food shortages that leave an estimated 40% of the population undernourished. But the regime has long been known to live in luxury. We don't know the cost of the vessels seen in the satellite imagery, but comparable luxury yachts run from tens of millions to over $100m (£75m). Kim's much smaller, 29-metre Princess yacht was previously estimated to be worth about $7m. While vessel locations alone cannot definitively establish the family's whereabouts, their movements - which overlap with gaps in Kim's public appearances - point to activities that would otherwise remain out of public view. Wonsan is where Kim Jong Un spent part of his childhood with his mother, according to biographers and intelligence reports, and one expert told the BBC the city has been associated with the family since his father Kim Jong Il's rule. A defector who served for 13 years guarding residences used by then leader Kim Jong Il - through the 1990s to the early 2000s - told the BBC the villas around Wonsan were used as a retreat by the elite. He recalls seeing dozens of children and teens waterskiing during summer. North Korean state media rarely publishes reports about Kim being on holiday, instead framing such visits as official inspections or guidance. But defectors interviewed by the BBC appeared to be aware that the family spent holidays in Wonsan, suggesting that at least some North Koreans knew about it. North Korean state media also claims Wonsan is home to high-rise hotels, restaurants, shops, sports facilities and water parks, and can accommodate nearly 20,000 visitors. State media and Russian outlets have published images of small groups of Russian tourists visiting the Wonsan Kalma resort, which opened in July 2025. Although developed to attract foreign visitors, the resort is also open to local tourists. Image source, AFP via Getty ImagesImage caption, North Korean tourists on a beach in Kalma A South Korean news report, citing an unnamed source, says some locals were offered four-night tour packages for around $100, a substantial sum for most North Koreans. The country's per capita GDP - around $667 in 2024, according to the UN - is a small fraction of South Korea's $36,227. For the majority of North Koreans, holidays are out of reach. And while a growing middle class does exist, they might not have much time for leisure. Defectors told the BBC that workers, office employees and cooperative farmers are legally entitled to 14 days of annual leave, but this is rarely followed. Taking consecutive days off to travel is unusual. People typically take weekend trips or travel during national holidays instead of designated "summer holidays". Even if leave is granted, travel itself is restricted, with official permission required for people to travel outside their city or county. Moving freely is sometimes as much a luxury as the holiday itself. Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption, Ordinary North Koreans struggle to earn a decent living The BBC tracked four large vessels around Wonsan, measuring approximately 50m, 55m, 60m and 80m. All four vessels repeatedly appeared around Kim's Wonsan villa this year. The largest vessel showed the clearest activity, moving from the dock to the waters off the Kalma Peninsula, where it has been since July. Two of the other vessels - 50m and 55m - were repeatedly seen until the end of August around Tae and Sin islands, close to Wonsan. Satellite images also showed four smaller boats alongside the 50m vessel. Image source, VantorImage caption, The 50m vessel was seen in waters near Tae island on 4 July 2026. Satellite imagery expert Jeong Seong-hak said the smaller boats ferried people, fuel and supplies to the larger vessel, adding that small islands like Tae and Sin offered "secluded maritime retreats where privacy can be maintained away from public view". The 60m vessel was repeatedly seen near Kim's Wonsan villa until as recently as last week. Though North Korea has never publicly disclosed the vessels' official ownership, BBC's analysis of historical satellite imagery found a large vessel with the same distinctive characteristics in Wonsan in 2002, when Kim Jong Il ruled North Korea. Former NBA star Dennis Rodman, who visited the North in 2013, told The Sun that he had spent much of his seven-day visit with Kim Jong Un around Wonsan, where they went jet-skiing and horse riding. He also described a 60m vessel they used as a cross between a ferry and a Disney boat. It is not clear if this is the same 60m boat pictured in the above satellite imagery. To most North Koreans, the life lived by the Kims and others who support the regime would seem not just extravagant but unimaginable. Especially because state propaganda is dedicated to presenting the "supreme leader" as a selfless man who always puts the nation first. "Kim Jong Un is supposed to be a 'leader of the people'," Ri Jong Ho says, "yet he has four luxury vessels like these while ordinary people are struggling just to get one meal a day."
