DUBAI, United Arab Emirates – Two alleged scammers have reportedly fled the country after pocketing AED 3.6 million (P61.7 million) from around 400 overseas Filipino workers (OFWs), in what could be the United Arab Emirates’ largest visa fraud case in recent years. The alleged suspects — Junie Sorsano, a prominent Dubai-based content creator for over a decade, and Ryan Ronel Baco — left the UAE during the first week of September and are now reportedly hiding in the Philippines.  An undetermined number of victims still in the Philippines have also organized to seek help from authorities. Sorsano serves as the CEO and founder of Trip Expert Business and Marketing Solutions, which opened on May 15, 2025, while Baco operates as the managing director.  The firm offered “legitimate and legal” freelance visa packages priced at AED 9,000 (P154,500) per applicant. The packages bypassed standard Philippine government safeguards, including contract verifications by the Migrant Workers Office (MWO) and the Overseas Employment Certificate (OEC), as well as the UAE-prescribed electronic salary transfer system. Prior to fleeing, Sorsano and Baco issued a joint public apology in September.  “We ask for your patience and kind consideration while we work through this challenging period,” the statement read. However, victims reported that the two have been completely unreachable since the statement was released. Furthermore, Trip Expert’s primary corporate office in Deira, Dubai, has been closed due to an alleged failure to pay rent. Victims noted that a major factor that drew them to the company was the involvement of two popular vloggers, who regularly appeared in advertisements promoting the merits of the freelance visa package. The digital creators, Abdul Hamid Bandon and Enrico Cardoniga, have strongly denied any involvement in the fraudulent scheme. On the contrary, both said the controversy has severely damaged their vlogging careers. Cardoniga, acting on legal advice, declined to go on record but disclosed that two major brands have already suspended their partnerships with him. Meanwhile, Bandon said he is waiting for the situation to “cool down” before speaking extensively. “ May mga nagtatanong sa akin (People are asking me),” he said. Ambrosio Brian Enciso III, Consul General at the Philippine Consulate General (PCG) in Dubai and the Northern Emirates, confirmed that authorities are actively investigating the scheme. “The Migrant Workers Office (MWO) Dubai, through its retained legal counsel, is providing appropriate support to individuals who have sought assistance,” Enciso said.  He noted that victims are receiving legal consultations and guidance on the documentary requirements needed by UAE authorities.  “Given the ongoing consultations and the need to respect the desire of the individuals concerned to maintain confidentiality, we are unable to provide further details at this time,” he said. PCG lawyer Eisa Khalife noted he is compiling evidence to formalize a case and may escalate the matter internationally.  “I may ask the Interpol (international police),” Khalife said, noting that he met with a delegation of 25 victims on October 7.  Interpol involvement would be required to extradite and bring the two suspects back to the UAE for prosecution. Many victims paid for the steep visa fees by using up their personal savings or taking out high-interest loans from lending agencies. They became suspicious only after Trip Expert abruptly scrubbed its digital presence. Cherry Laroga, an applicant, noticed the red flags when the company’s heavy stream of Facebook advertisements suddenly stopped.  “ September 24 yung time na nag-scroll ako sa Facebook, ‘di na lumalabas ads nila. Duon ako nagtaka kaya naghanap ako sa TikTok, dun may nabasa akong comment na ‘wag bumili ng visa diyan kasi marami ang di na-process…kaya nag-message ako sa agent ko nung same day, ” said Laroga. (It was September 24 when I scrolled on Facebook and noticed that their ads were not showing anymore. I grew suspicious and searched TikTok, where I saw comments warning people not to buy visas from them because applications weren’t being processed. I messaged my agent that same day.) She said her agent responded honestly. “’I will be transparent with you, ma’am,’” Laroga said, recalling the agent’s response. “ Wala daw pong funds ang company… kaya pati kaming empleyado walang sahod at hindi rin matapos ang application ninyo sa visa. ’” (The company reportedly has no funds…that’s why even us, employees, do not have salaries anymore, and it’s the reason why your visa application hasn’t been processed.) The fallout quickly escalated across social media, prompting victims to storm Trip Expert’s abandoned corporate offices demanding refunds and report the incident to the PCG. The victims are mostly domestic helpers, caregivers, and retail sales staff — who sought freelance visas to legally pursue independent, self-sponsored employment. Gwendolyn Cajutol said she has accumulated more than AED11,000 in fines for overstaying because she still does not have her Emirates ID due to the scam.  “ Fully paid na ko sa visa. Sakit ng naranasan ko ngayon. Masakit. Mahirap tanggapin po ,” she said.  (I’ve already paid in full for the visa. What I’m going through right now is so painful. It hurts. It’s hard to accept.) Fatima, who requested anonymity, said she had trusted the visa company because they were run by Filipinos. She had also felt assured by their regular social media advertisements. “ Noong una po, sila mismo ang sobrang kulit. Panay ang tawag at chat nila sa akin para kumbinsihin akong mag-avail ng kanilang self-sponsored visa processing ,” she recalled.  (At first, they were the ones who were really persistent. They kept calling and messaging me to convince me to avail of their self-sponsored visa processing service.) “ Dahil mga kababayan ko rin po sila at mukhang maayos at legitimate ang kanilang operation, nagtiwala po ako, ” Fatima said, adding that she paid AED9,000 in May this year. “ Binayaran ko po agad ng cash kasi sabi nila hindi daw ipa-process kapag hindi fully paid. Ang usapan po namin ay matatapos ang proseso within approximately 60 working days o dalawang buwan .” (Since they are also my Filipinos and their operation seems to be sound and legitimate, I trusted them. I paid in cash immediately because they said the process wouldn’t move forward unless it was fully paid. We agreed that the process would be completed within approximately 60 working days, or two months.) Fatima said things changed after she made the payment. “ Kung anu-anong dahilan na po ang sinasabi nila. Paulit-ulit nilang sinasabi na delayed daw sa authorities, kaya patuloy lang kaming naghihintay at umaasa. Ngayon po, magli-limang buwan na, pero wala pa rin akong residency visa, ” she said. (They kept giving all sorts of reasons. They repeatedly claimed that things were being delayed by the authorities, so we just kept waiting and hoping. It has now been nearly five months, yet I still do not have a residency visa.) Her grace period has since expired, forcing her to exit the UAE to Oman twice on costly tourist visa extensions. Fatima’s UAE bank account has also been frozen. She has been jobless for two months, and she cannot send money home to her family.  “ Hindi na po ako halos makatulog. Hindi na ako makakain nang maayos dahil sa kakaisip kung ano ang mangyayari sa visa ko, sa pera ko at sa kinabukasan ko dito sa Dubai ,” Fatima said, noting that she even borrowed the AED 9,000 needed to pay the visa fee. (I can barely sleep or eat properly from worrying about my visa, my money, and my future in Dubai.) “ Kami po ang mga OFW na araw-araw nagtatrabaho at nagsasakripisyo para makaipon. Nagtiwala kami dahil mga kapwa Pilipino namin ang kausap namin ,” added Fatima. (We are OFWs who work and make sacrifices every single day in order to save money. We placed our trust in them) because we were dealing with fellow Filipinos.) “ Mas masakit po dahil sa ibang bansa na nga po kami, kapwa Pilipino pa sana ang aasahan namin. Kung sino pa ang kapwa Pilipino mo sa abroad, sila pa pala ang makakapagbigay sa ‘yo ng ganitong problema .” “ Gusto lang po namin ng hustisya .” (It hurts even more because we’re already in a foreign country, so we’re expecting to be able to rely on fellow Filipinos. It turns out that the very people you’d expect to support you, your fellow Filipinos abroad, are the ones who end up causing you this kind of trouble. We just want justice.) – Rappler.com Dig Deeper Add to Preferred Sources Share in Chat Facebook X (Twitter) Copy Link Related Topics Dubai United Arab Emirates {{ item.sitename }} {{ item.primarytopic }} {{ item.primarytopic }} {{ item.title }}

articles.title: US Warns Against Russian Diesel Deal: Sanctions Risk
articles.content: Ukrainian president Volodymyr Zelensky said on Friday (16 October) that the US-Russia ‘diesel deal’ came as a surprise and could lead to further sanctions relief for Moscow. “We cannot treat the agreements concerning diesel and coal as isolated cases … gas could be next. I am absolutely convinced of that,” Zelensky told reporters in Brussels, after meeting with EU leaders. “The risks I am talking about are clear: sanctions could be progressively eased,” he warned. EU leaders are expected to “regret” the diesel deal in their summit conclusions, while discussions on a new package of sanctions against Russia are still underway. “It is not a time to release sanctions on Russia,” said EU Council president Antonio Costa on Friday, alongside EU Commission president Ursula von der Leyen and Zelensky before the discussion with EU leaders. “We will not lift any sanctions unless Russia ends the war,” confirmed von der Leyen, adding that Europe will keep working on “pressuring Russia”. Europe has adopted 21 packages of sanctions on Russia since the beginning of the war, alongside the listing of thousands of individuals and entities, and is currently working on the 22nd. But one Ukrainian senior diplomat told EUobserver that the coming months could be crucial to agree on more sanctions against Moscow, since February is seen as a possible deadline given the upcoming 2027 French presidential elections . Russia’s economy has come under growing pressure from Western sanctions. Although a month-on-month decrease in exports was observed (six percent for fossil fuels, eight percent for crude oil), the US diesel deal could offer Moscow a potential lifeline. The diesel deal is widely seen as a way to restart peace talks. At the same time, the United States is pushing Kyiv and Moscow toward a negotiated settlement, which puts Ukraine under growing pressure to come to the table, even though any deal could force it to make painful concessions. Zelensky, however, has warned against any deal that would compromise Ukraine’s sovereignty or territorial integrity. "Putin plans to stick around much longer. He is building a Russia that looks like North Korea," he wrote on X. Instead, the Ukrainian president has turned to European “real leaders”, seeking to shore up their political and military support and strengthen Kyiv’s position in any future negotiations.  And in the words of von der Leyen, Europe is already helping Ukraine to prepare for “winter-isation”, which for Zelensky should translate into more funds and defence support. This week, the commission disembursed €2.9bn to Kyiv to purchase drones, air defence systems, missiles, radars, electronic warfare systems and ammunition, as part of the EU’s €90bn loan, backed by EU leaders last year.  But Kyiv has warned it will need tens of billions more to continue fighting against Russia, as the war intensifies on the front lines and the number of attacks in Ukrainian cities increases. Ukraine’s defence needs are estimated for 2026 around €23bn and Kyiv still needs to fund a hole of roughly €69.3bn for 2027. “We will have to increase the funding once again,” German chancellor Friedrich Merz said on Thursday before meeting EU leaders in Brussels.  To read this story, log in or subscribe Enjoy access to all articles and 25 years of archives, comment and gift articles. articles.title: StarCraft AI 'Gemini 4 Argon' Shows Advanced Play
articles.content: TL;DR StarSkirmish is a benchmark where LLMs write bots for StarCraft: Brood War Each LLM gets one hour to write a Protoss bot in C++, which is then evaluated against other LLMs' bots and established human written bots StarSkirmish tests long horizon reasoning and agentic coding as LLMs must incorporate learnings from practice games to improve their StarCraft bot StarSkirmish Bench v0.2 The StarSkirmish Bench evaluates how strong of a StarCraft bot can each LLM write given 1 hour of wall clock time. v0.2 updates StarSkirmish Bench v0.1 with flagship models from OpenAI, Anthropic, Google and Meta, each running in its lab's 1st party CLI harness. An LLM’s score reflects its win rate against a roster of competitive human written bots and demo bots. StarSkirmish Bench v0.2 1 hour runs, in its 1st party CLI harness. Scores are average win rates (0–100) of each model's 5 runs against a roster of competitive human written bots. Gemini 4 Argon runs at high , the highest reasoning effort available to it; every other model runs at max . GPT-6 Astra is the top scoring StarSkirmish Bench v0.2 LLM, a clear step ahead of GPT-6.1 Sol in second. Gemini 4 Argon, Claude Opus 5.5 and Claude Fable 5.1 are functionally tied behind them, all scoring between 37 and 39. StarSkirmish Bench vs. Cost StarSkirmish Bench score against the average API cost of one 1 hour run. Cost is on a log scale. Muse Wonder Full's pricing is based on Muse Wonder's API pricing. GPT-6.1 Sol offers uniquely good value: it is the only LLM in the most attractive quadrant, scoring second at just over a tenth of GPT-6 Astra's cost per run. No Signs of Saturating The strongest human written bots are still well ahead of every model. Against Stardust, PurpleWave and BananaBrain, the best model, GPT-6 Astra, wins only 7% of its games. Win rates vs the top human written bots Average win rate of each model's 5 bots against top human written bots Stardust, PurpleWave, and BananaBrain. 1 hour reasoning limits are a factor, but these matches are played on three 2 player maps. Real human written bot tournament conditions are significantly harder. New AI Model Highlights Google and Meta's new flagships replace v0.1's Gemini 3.8 Flash and Muse Spark 1.3: Gemini 4 Argon places 3rd, and Muse Wonder Full 7th. GPT-6 Astra and Claude Opus 5.5 were covered in v0.1 . AI Model Behaviors Each run's agent trace records how it spent its hour. The strongest predictor of a model's score is how much it practiced against the 7 strongest bots on the roster. Win Rates vs. Practice Against Strong Bots StarSkirmish Bench score against the number of practice games a model's median run played against the 7 strongest roster bots during the hour. The dashed line is a linear fit across the 9 models. GPT-6 Astra, GPT-6.1 Sol and Gemini 4 Argon start playing these bots early in the hour, while their own bots still lose to them. Muse Wonder Full, Claude Haiku 5.5 and GPT-6 Luna rarely or never do. Claude Fable 5.1 is the outlier: it scores 37 while practicing almost entirely against weaker bots. Run-to-Run Variance Win rates of each model's 5 runs. Each dot is one run's final bot; the line spans the lowest to the highest run, the bar marks their mean (the model's Bench score) and the band one standard deviation (σ). Results also vary between runs of the same model. Gemini 4 Argon varies far more than the other labs' flagships: its best and worst runs are 18 points apart, against 9 for GPT-6 Astra and 8 for Claude Opus 5.5. Objective Each LLM writes a Protoss bot in C++ against BWAPI 4.4.0 , played on OpenBW . Games are Protoss versus Protoss on three ladder maps: Heartbreak Ridge, Benzene and Destination. A game ends when one side's buildings are all destroyed. Games that reach the 60 minute cap (86,400 frames) are decided as on the BASIL ladder: the higher kills + razings score wins. The LLM starts from a skeleton bot that only mines, with the source code of the three demo bots and two standard bot libraries: FAP, a combat simulator, and BWEM, a map analyzer. Whatever is in its bot folder when the hour ends is its final bot, so it has to keep the bot compiling. The LLM has tools to compile its bot, play practice games, and read each game's summary, transcript and its bot's own log. Practice opponents are grouped into tiers: D (the three demo bots), C and B (three mid-ranked human written bots each), A (BananaBrain, Locutus) and S (Stardust, PurpleWave). Tournament Setup LLM bots Opponents Games Games / pair Each model's 5 final bots play each of the 13 roster bots, the 10 competitive human written bots and the 3 demo bots, 6 times on each map, on fresh seeds. Unlike v0.1, the LLM bots don't play each other. Harness and Reasoning StarSkirmish Bench v0.1 ran every model in the same harness at 'high' reasoning. v0.2 runs each model in its lab's 1st party CLI harness at the highest reasoning setting it offers. Harness v0.1 ran every model in one neutral 3rd party harness; v0.2 runs each lab's models in its 1st party CLI harness. Both versions give each model 1 hour. Inspect ReAct deepagent Claude Opus 5.5 GPT-6 Astra, Sol, Luna Gemini 3.8 Flash Muse Spark 1.3 Claude Code Claude Opus 5.5, Fable 5.1, Sonnet 5.5, Haiku 5.5 Codex GPT-6 Astra, GPT-6.1 Sol, GPT-6 Luna Antigravity CLI Gemini 4 Argon Muse Code Muse Wonder Full CLI versions: Claude Code 2.1.296, Codex 0.162.1, Antigravity CLI 1.3.5 and Muse Code 1.4.7. Reasoning Effort v0.1 ran every model at high reasoning effort; v0.2 runs them at max. v0.1 Low Medium High XHigh Max High v0.2 Low Medium High XHigh Max Max Gemini 4 Argon runs at high , the highest effort supported. Every v0.2 harness compacts the model's context at about 250k tokens. When a conversation nears that point, the CLI condenses it and the model carries on. Codex, OpenAI's CLI, for example, gives the GPT models its default 272k token window and triggers compression once 90% filled. The CLIs' web search and web fetch tools are turned off, and the agent has no other internet access. The CLI is installed before the clock starts, and the hour counts from when the agent starts. There is no submit tool: the harness collects the bot when the time runs out. Scoring v0.2 replaces v0.1's Elo ratings with plain win rates. A bot's score is its win rate over its tournament games, and a model's StarSkirmish Bench score is the average of its 5 bots' scores, from 0 (every game lost) to 100 (every game won). Because every bot plays the same fixed roster, its games don't depend on the other LLM bots in the field. They all run in parallel, and a new model's bots can be scored without replaying anyone else's. A fixed roster also keeps the bar the same over time, so scores from different model generations are more directly comparable than Elo ratings fitted within one field. Benchmark Correlations StarSkirmish no longer tracks the most widely reported evals. It barely moves with the Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index (ρ 0.26), where GPT-6 Astra, the top model here, only ties for 4th of these 9 models. It has also drifted away from Terminal-Bench 4.0, which it tracked closely in v0.1. Claude Sonnet 5.5 and Muse Wonder Full both rank near the top of Terminal-Bench 4.0 but near the bottom here. Benchmark Correlation Each model's StarSkirmish Bench score against its Vals IOI and WeirdML v3 scores, with the Spearman ρ between them. The dashed line is the best straight-line fit. WeirdML v3 scores 7 of the 9 models: Gemini 4 Argon and Muse Wonder Full have not been included at time of writing. StarSkirmish still tracks Vals IOI, olympiad programming problems solved in C++, and WeirdML, an independent benchmark of unusual machine learning coding tasks. One reading is that the most heavily benchmarked evals have become targets that models are tuned for, while less targeted tests of long horizon, difficult coding tasks still move together.

articles.title: Don’t Let a Crypto Inheritance Get Stuck
articles.content: Save Story Save this story Save Story Save this story know has cryptocurrency that you might inherit, let me just say ahoy matey! I hope your pirate spirit is alive and your treasure-hunting skills sharp, because that's what it might take to get those assets. And if you're the one holding crypto, know that if you do nothing, it's very possible those funds will die with you. In the US, cryptocurrency is considered a digital asset rather than money in terms of probate and estate law. With money and physical assets, you can sign a beneficiary form and create an estate plan or write a last will and testament naming who should get what when you die. With digital assets, however, the law says we should not assume that a deceased person wanted their private materials—everything from emails to photos—given to another person unless they explicitly said so. This puts cryptocurrency, as a digital asset, in an awkward position. The options for arranging a transfer of cryptocurrency upon one's death or incapacitation breaks down by one big division: whether the crypto is held by a custodian or in a noncustodial crypto wallet . Two Types of Wallets A custodian or custodial wallet means a third party, such as a bank or a cryptocurrency marketplace, holds and manages the assets for you. Typically, transferring assets after death is much easier with a custodian, especially if it's a bank. Noncustodial wallets eliminate the middleman and let a person hold their assets directly. For crypto enthusiasts whose interest in digital currency is driven by a distaste for the traditional banking system, then using a noncustodial wallet is kind of the whole point. Noncustodial wallets can be software or hardware-based. It can even be a piece of paper with the instructions and passwords for accessing the cryptocurrency on it. (I use "password" here and throughout to refer to any string of letters, numbers, and characters needed to gain access to someone’s cryptocurrency.) Whatever kind of noncustodial wallet you choose, passing on your assets will require a DIY solution. Pros and Cons of a Custodial Wallet When you use a third-party custodian to hold your cryptocurrency, you can choose one that has a beneficiary process in place. Charles Schwab and Chase are just two examples of large, well-known financial institutions that offer crypto services and have experience transferring assets after death. Schwab, for example, houses its cryptocurrency services within brokerage accounts. Signing a beneficiary form for a brokerage account applies to the crypto account as well. One and done. Another benefit of using a bank is that at least three entities know you have an account: the bank, the government, and the credit reporting bureaus. Avenues exist for finding the banked money of deceased people. With a noncustodial wallet, this is not at all the case. Note that cryptocurrency accounts, even when held through a bank, are not FDIC-insured. Other custodians include crypto marketplaces, such as Coinbase, and peer-to-peer payment services, like PayPal. Neither Coinbase nor PayPal have beneficiary forms as of this writing, though they do have a clear process for proving a person is entitled to a decedent's account. In both cases, you must have legal documents saying you are the executor of the estate (for PayPal) or are entitled to inherit the account (Coinbase), as well as a death certificate and other documentation. So the process is clunky and takes some advance planning, but it's still straightforward. How many disadvantages there are to using a custodian depends on your outlook. As mentioned, crypto enthusiasts who eschew traditional banking may not see any value in using a custodian. Banks require ID, so you cannot hold the crypto anonymously. Banks and many other custodians report your transactions to the federal government, holding you accountable to an honest tax filing. Custodial wallets also cost money. They typically charge transaction fees, usually a small percentage of each trade. Pros and Cons of a Noncustodial Wallet The primary benefit of a noncustodial wallet is that everything is in your control. You hold the assets directly. You're responsible for knowing and keeping safe the information you need to access your assets. You also have to come up with a plan for informing your beneficiaries that a crypto account exists and making sure they can access it. The first and biggest problem is that if you get locked out while you're alive, it's game over . "If you lose your cryptographic key, there's no company that you can appeal to," says Benjamin Orzeske, chief counsel for Uniform Law Commission and a staff attorney for the Revised Uniform Fiduciary Access to Digital Assets Act, the law that guides how digital inheritance is handled in most states. The other major hurdle is that your fiduciary needs to know the crypto exists. No government or credit reporting bureau has a record of you holding the account. The only people who know are the ones you tell. Now let's get procedural. Because of how the blockchain works, you must figure out a secure way to give your heirs instructions for obtaining the assets. Your system has to be safe. It doesn't come with any backups or failsafes unless you create them. And whether you can test your system to make sure it works before you die will require a huge amount of trust. Ideas from Reddit users for how to build a system for passing on cryptocurrency include email dead-man switches, printed instructions given to a trusted person, and splitting instructions across two people who will need to come together to obtain access. All these solutions could work but have obvious flaws: the failure of an email system, a trusted person dying alongside you, someone forgetting you gave them instructions, and so forth. The best option may be to put the bulk of the instructions into your estate plan, including your named fiduciary, but crucially omitting any passwords. As Catherine Hodder, a senior attorney editor at FindLaw, explained to me, “The will is a public document,” and you should never put any usernames or passwords in your will. An excellent place to put your password is inside a safe-deposit box at a bank. The existence of the deposit box should also be listed in your will. Some crypto owners have suggested stamping the password into a metal plate, which I suppose is a fine idea if you don't trust ink and paper to last longer than you. One potential flaw is still that you can't do a dry run to make sure your system works unless you trust your fiduciary completely. Something as simple as needing your fingerprint to unlock a device could spell the end of your plan. An objection that some staunchly anti-capitalistic investors may have is that by including your cryptocurrency in your estate plan, you've returned it to the realm of traditional law and governance. Then again, you'll be dead.
